statement: Let $f$ be a [cusp form](c:cusp-form) of integer weight $k$ for a subgroup $\Gamma$ of finite index in the [modular group](c:modular-group), with [q-expansion](c:q-expansion) $\sum_{n\ge1}a_nq_h^n$, where $q_h=e^{2\pi i\tau/h}$ and $h$ is the width of the cusp $\infty$. Then $a_n=O(n^{k/2})$ as $n\to\infty$.

hypotheses.text: $\Gamma$ is a subgroup of finite index in the [modular group](c:modular-group) $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$.
$f$ is a [cusp form](c:cusp-form) of integer weight $k$ for $\Gamma$: holomorphic, of weight $k$, and vanishing at every cusp.

conclusion: The coefficients of the [q-expansion](c:q-expansion) of $f$ at $\infty$ satisfy $|a_n|\le Cn^{k/2}$ for all $n\ge1$, with $C$ depending on $f$ only.

formal.difference: mathlib proves the bound for an arithmetic subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb R)$, which contains the finite-index subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. The q-expansion there uses the strict width of $\infty$.

proofs.name: Coefficients on a horizontal line
proofs.slogan: Bound the cusp form by a power of the imaginary part, then read each coefficient from an integral along a horizontal line.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for every integer weight $k$ (for $k\le0$ a cusp form is zero and the bound is trivial). The constant $C$ depends on $f$ and $\Gamma$ only.

roles.why: Finite index gives finitely many cusps and a fundamental domain that is a finite union of translates of the standard one.
The transformation law gives invariance, holomorphy gives the Fourier series, and vanishing at the cusps gives decay.

steps.slogan: Show that the weighted size $g(\tau)=|f(\tau)|\,y^{k/2}$ is invariant under $\Gamma$, with $y=\mathrm{Im}\,\tau$.
steps.detail: For $\gamma\in\Gamma$ with bottom row $(c,d)$, the weight $k$ law gives $|f(\gamma\tau)|=|c\tau+d|^k|f(\tau)|$. Also $\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma\tau=y/|c\tau+d|^2$. The factors $|c\tau+d|$ cancel in $g(\gamma\tau)=g(\tau)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $g$ is bounded on the upper half plane because it tends to zero at every cusp.
steps.detail: A fundamental domain of $\Gamma$ is a finite union of translates $\sigma_jF$ of the standard domain $F$. At each cusp the form has a $q$-expansion without constant term, so $g\to0$ as $y\to\infty$ on each $\sigma_jF$. A continuous function that tends to zero at the ends of each piece is bounded, and invariance extends the bound: $|f(\tau)|\le Cy^{-k/2}$.

steps.slogan: Write each coefficient $a_n$ as a [Fourier coefficient](c:fourier-coefficients) of $f$ along a horizontal line.
steps.detail: The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) and $f(\tau+h)=f(\tau)$, so $f=\sum a_ne^{2\pi in\tau/h}$. Integrating over one period gives $a_n=\frac1h\int_0^hf(x+iy)\,e^{-2\pi in(x+iy)/h}\,dx$ for every $y>0$.

steps.slogan: Bound $|a_n|$ by the size of $f$ on the line and the factor $e^{2\pi ny/h}$.
steps.detail: The integrand of step 3 has modulus at most $Cy^{-k/2}e^{2\pi ny/h}$ by step 2. Hence $|a_n|\le Cy^{-k/2}e^{2\pi ny/h}$ for every $y>0$.

steps.slogan: Choose the height $y=1/n$ to get $|a_n|\le Ce^{2\pi/h}n^{k/2}$.
steps.detail: For $n\ge1$ put $y=1/n$ in the bound of step 4. Then $y^{-k/2}=n^{k/2}$ and $e^{2\pi ny/h}=e^{2\pi/h}$, so $a_n=O(n^{k/2})$.

concepts.c:cusp-form: Vanishing at the cusps makes the weighted size tend to zero there.
concepts.c:modular-group: The group action gives the invariance and the finite fundamental domain.
concepts.c:q-expansion: The coefficients $a_n$ of the q-expansion are the quantities that the proof bounds.
concepts.c:fourier-coefficients: Each q-expansion coefficient equals a Fourier coefficient of $f$ on a horizontal line.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy makes $f$ equal to its Fourier series on every horizontal line.

source.note: mathlib bounds $|f|$ by $C/(\mathrm{Im}\,\tau)^{k/2}$ (CuspFormClass.exists_bound, through the Petersson norm) and then applies qExpansion_coeff_isBigO_of_norm_isBigO, which integrates along the line at height $1/n$.

statement: Let $f$ be piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $|f(t)|\le Me^{ct}$, and let $F(s)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ be its [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform) for $s>c$. If the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $L=\lim_{t\to0^+}f(t)$ exists, then $\lim_{s\to\infty}sF(s)=L$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is piecewise continuous with $|f(t)|\le Me^{ct}$, so its [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform) $F(s)$ exists for $s>c$.
The one-sided [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $L=\lim_{t\to0^+}f(t)$ exists.

proofs.name: Weighted average
proofs.slogan: Write $sF(s)-L$ as an average of $f-L$ against the density $se^{-st}$, then split the average at a small time $\delta$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for real or complex $f$; the proof needs no derivative of $f$. A jump of $f$ away from $0$ does not matter.

roles.why: The exponential bound makes the tail integral small and makes $F(s)$ exist for large $s$.
The limit makes $f-L$ small on a short interval $(0,\delta)$.

steps.slogan: Write $sF(s)-L$ as an integral against the density $se^{-st}$.
steps.detail: For $s>0$ we have $\int_0^\infty se^{-st}\,dt=1$, so $L=\int_0^\infty se^{-st}L\,dt$. Subtracting this from $sF(s)=\int_0^\infty se^{-st}f(t)\,dt$ gives $sF(s)-L=\int_0^\infty se^{-st}\,(f(t)-L)\,dt$ for $s>\max(c,0)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the part of the integral on $(0,\delta)$ by a small number $\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: Given $\varepsilon>0$, the definition of the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) gives $\delta>0$ with $|f(t)-L|<\varepsilon$ for $0<t<\delta$. Then $\left|\int_0^\delta se^{-st}(f(t)-L)\,dt\right|\le\varepsilon\int_0^\delta se^{-st}\,dt\le\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Bound the part of the integral on $(\delta,\infty)$ by a term that tends to zero.
steps.detail: For $t>\delta$ we have $|f(t)-L|\le Me^{ct}+|L|$. For $s>c$ the integral of $se^{-st}$ times this bound over $(\delta,\infty)$ equals $\frac{sM}{s-c}e^{-(s-c)\delta}+|L|e^{-s\delta}$, which tends to $0$ as $s\to\infty$.

steps.slogan: Add the two bounds to get $|sF(s)-L|<2\varepsilon$ for large $s$.
steps.detail: For $s$ large the part on $(\delta,\infty)$ is below $\varepsilon$, and the part on $(0,\delta)$ is below $\varepsilon$ for every $s$. So $|sF(s)-L|<2\varepsilon$, and $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, so $\lim_{s\to\infty}sF(s)=L$.

concepts.c:laplace-transform: The function $sF(s)$ is the transform multiplied by $s$, rewritten as an average.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-function: The limit at $0^+$ makes $f-L$ small near $0$.

source.note: A direct approximate-identity argument; the textbook proof through the transform of $f'$ needs $f'$ to be transformable as well.

statement: Let $A$, $B$, $P$ lie on a [circle](c:circle) with center $O$ in an oriented Euclidean plane, with $P\ne A$ and $P\ne B$. Then the central angle at $O$ is twice the [inscribed angle](c:inscribed-angle) at $P$: $\angle(OA,OB)=2\angle(PA,PB)$ as [oriented angles](c:oriented-angle) modulo $2\pi$.

hypotheses.text: The points $A$, $B$, $P$ lie on a [circle](c:circle) with center $O$ and radius $r$.
The point $P$ differs from $A$ and from $B$, so the angle at $P$ is defined.

formal.difference: The declaration says that two inscribed angles on one chord are equal modulo $\pi$ (twice each angle agrees), a corollary of this theorem. The theorem itself is the neighboring lemma Orientation.oangle_eq_two_zsmul_oangle_sub_of_norm_eq_real.

proofs.name: Isosceles triangles at the center
proofs.slogan: Express the central angle through the base angles of the two isosceles triangles $OPA$ and $OPB$, then merge the base angles into the inscribed angle.
proofs.scope: Oriented angles modulo $2\pi$, with no case split on the position of $P$. If $A=B$ both sides are $0$.

roles.why: Equal radii $|OP|=|OA|=|OB|=r$ make the triangles $OPA$ and $OPB$ isosceles.
The vectors $P-A$ and $P-B$ are nonzero, so the base angles and the angle at $P$ exist.

steps.slogan: Put the center $O$ at the origin, so that $|P|=|A|=|B|=r$.
steps.detail: A translation keeps the oriented angles between difference vectors. Then $\angle(OA,OB)=\angle(A,B)$, and the three vectors $P$, $A$, $B$ have length $r$.

steps.slogan: Write each apex angle at $O$ as $\pi$ minus twice a base angle.
steps.detail: In the isosceles triangle $OPB$ the apex angle at $O$ is $\pi$ minus twice the base angle: $\angle(P,B)=\pi-2\angle(P-B,P)$. The triangle $OPA$ gives $\angle(P,A)=\pi-2\angle(P-A,P)$.

steps.slogan: Split the central angle at $O$ as a difference of two angles from $OP$.
steps.detail: Oriented angles add, so the angle from $P$ to $A$ plus the angle from $A$ to $B$ is the angle from $P$ to $B$: $\angle(P,A)+\angle(A,B)=\angle(P,B)$. Hence $\angle(A,B)=\angle(P,B)-\angle(P,A)$.

steps.slogan: Substitute the base angles and merge them into the inscribed angle.
steps.detail: By steps 2 and 3, $\angle(A,B)=2\big(\angle(P-A,P)-\angle(P-B,P)\big)=2\angle(P-A,P-B)$, because oriented angles subtract. Negating both vectors keeps the angle, so $\angle(P-A,P-B)=\angle(A-P,B-P)=\angle(PA,PB)$.

concepts.c:circle: Equal radii from the center give the isosceles triangles.
concepts.c:inscribed-angle: The angle at $P$ on the circle is the angle that the theorem halves.
concepts.c:oriented-angle: Oriented angles add and subtract without a case split, and they carry the sign.

source.note: mathlib proves the central angle lemma oangle_eq_two_zsmul_oangle_sub_of_norm_eq_real from the isosceles lemma oangle_eq_pi_sub_two_zsmul_oangle_sub_of_norm_eq and the angle addition lemmas oangle_sub_left and oangle_sub_right; the declaration applies it at two points.

statement: Let $E/F$ be an [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension), $\sigma\colon F\to F'$ an isomorphism of fields and $\overline{F'}$ an [algebraic closure](c:algebraic-closure) of $F'$. Then $\sigma$ extends to a field embedding $\tau\colon E\to\overline{F'}$, an isomorphism of $E$ onto a subfield of $\overline{F'}$.

hypotheses.text: $E$ is an [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension) of $F$.
$\sigma\colon F\to F'$ is an isomorphism of fields.
$\overline{F'}$ is an [algebraic closure](c:algebraic-closure) of $F'$, so it is algebraically closed.

conclusion: There is a field embedding $\tau\colon E\to\overline{F'}$ with $\tau|_F=\sigma$.

proofs.name: Zorn's lemma
proofs.slogan: Order the partial extensions of $\sigma$ by inclusion, take a maximal one with Zorn's lemma, and show that its domain is all of $E$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, with no case split. The corollaries (splitting fields of $p$ and $\sigma p$ are isomorphic, and algebraic closures are unique up to isomorphism) follow by counting roots and are not proved here.

roles.why: Each element of $E$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial over the current domain, so it has a minimal polynomial.
The isomorphism $\sigma$, followed by the inclusion $F'\subseteq\overline{F'}$, is the first partial extension.
Algebraic closedness gives a root of every nonconstant polynomial, which is the image of the new element.

steps.slogan: Collect the partial extensions $(K,\tau)$ of $\sigma$ into a partially ordered set $\mathcal P$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal P$ consist of pairs $(K,\tau)$ with $F\subseteq K\subseteq E$ a subfield and $\tau\colon K\to\overline{F'}$ a field embedding with $\tau|_F=\sigma$. Order by $(K,\tau)\le(K',\tau')$ when $K\subseteq K'$ and $\tau'|_K=\tau$. The pair $(F,\sigma)$ is in $\mathcal P$, so $\mathcal P$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Bound each chain of $\mathcal P$ by the union of its fields, and take a maximal pair.
steps.detail: For a chain $(K_i,\tau_i)$ the union $K=\bigcup K_i$ is a subfield of $E$, and the maps $\tau_i$ agree on overlaps, so they define one embedding $\tau$ of $K$. This pair bounds the chain, so Zorn's lemma gives a maximal pair $(K,\tau)$.

steps.slogan: Extend an embedding $\tau$ of $K$ over one element $\alpha\in E\setminus K$.
steps.detail: Let $p$ be the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) of $\alpha$ over $K$, and let $\tau p$ be $p$ with $\tau$ applied to its coefficients. The polynomial $\tau p$ has degree at least $1$, so it has a root $\beta\in\overline{F'}$. The map $K[x]/(p)\to\overline{F'}$ with $x\mapsto\beta$ extends $\tau$ to $K(\alpha)\cong K[x]/(p)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude from maximality that the domain of the maximal pair is $E$.
steps.detail: If $K\ne E$, step 3 gives a pair $(K(\alpha),\tau')$ in $\mathcal P$ above $(K,\tau)$, which contradicts maximality. So $K=E$, and $\tau\colon E\to\overline{F'}$ extends $\sigma$.

concepts.c:algebraic-extension: Algebraic elements have minimal polynomials, which lets each step add one element.
concepts.c:algebraic-closure: An algebraically closed target has a root for every polynomial $\tau p$.
concepts.c:minimal-polynomial: The minimal polynomial describes the field generated by the new element.

source.note: The standard Zorn's lemma argument, as in Lang, Algebra, chapter V, theorem 2.8.

statement: Let $M$ be a [semisimple module](c:is-semisimple-module) over a ring $R$ (for example a [simple module](c:is-simple-module)), and let $f\colon M\to M$ commute with every $R$-endomorphism of $M$. For every finite set $s\subseteq M$ there is $r\in R$ with $f(m)=rm$ for all $m\in s$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a [semisimple module](c:is-semisimple-module) over the ring $R$.
The map $f$ is linear over the [endomorphism ring](c:endomorphism-ring) $D=\mathrm{End}_R(M)$: $f(\varphi(m))=\varphi(f(m))$ for all $\varphi\in D$.
The set $s\subseteq M$ is [finite](c:finite-set).

conclusion: Some $r\in R$ satisfies $f(m)=rm$ for every $m\in s$.

proofs.name: Direct summand in a power of M
proofs.slogan: Pack the finite set into one vector of a power of $M$, split off the submodule it generates, and push the commuting map through the projection.
proofs.scope: The whole statement; for $s=\emptyset$ the choice $r=0$ works. For a simple module $D$ is a division ring (Schur's lemma), and the statement says that $R$ is dense in $\mathrm{End}_D(M)$.

roles.why: Semisimplicity makes every submodule of the power $M^s$ a direct summand.
Commuting with $D$ makes the diagonal map commute with every $R$-endomorphism of $M^s$, in particular with the projection.
Finiteness of $s$ makes $M^s$ a finite direct sum of copies of $M$, which is semisimple.

steps.slogan: Pack the finite set $s$ into one vector $x$ of the power $M^s$.
steps.detail: Let $M^s$ be the direct sum of copies of $M$ indexed by $s$, and let $x=(m)_{m\in s}$. A finite direct sum of [semisimple modules](c:is-semisimple-module) is semisimple, so $M^s$ is semisimple.

steps.slogan: Choose a complement of $Rx$ in $M^s$ and form the projection $p$ onto $Rx$.
steps.detail: Every submodule of a semisimple module has a complement, so $M^s=Rx\oplus C$. Let $p$ be the projection onto $Rx$ along $C$. It is $R$-linear and $p(x)=x$.

steps.slogan: Show that the diagonal map $f^s$ commutes with $p$.
steps.detail: Let $f^s(v)_m=f(v_m)$. An $R$-endomorphism of $M^s$ is a matrix $(\varphi_{mn})$ with entries in $D$. Since $f$ is $D$-linear, $f^s$ commutes with every such matrix, so $f^sp=pf^s$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f^s(x)$ lies in the submodule $Rx$.
steps.detail: We have $f^s(x)=f^s(p(x))=p(f^s(x))$, and the image of $p$ is $Rx$. So $f^s(x)\in Rx$.

steps.slogan: Read the scalar $r$ from $f^s(x)=rx$ coordinate by coordinate.
steps.detail: Write $f^s(x)=rx$ with $r\in R$. The coordinate of index $m$ gives $f(m)=rm$ for every $m\in s$.

concepts.c:is-semisimple-module: Semisimplicity supplies the complement of $Rx$ and so the projection.
concepts.c:is-simple-module: A simple module is the basic example of a semisimple module.
concepts.c:endomorphism-ring: The map $f$ commutes with this ring, which gives the commutation with $p$.
concepts.c:finite-set: A finite set gives a finite direct sum, which stays semisimple.

source.note: mathlib takes $x$ in the power $s\to M$ (Finsupp.equivFunOnFinite), a complement of $Rx$ from exists_isCompl, the projection with projection_apply_mem, and the diagonal map End.ringHomEndFinsupp.

statement: Let $X$ be a connected pointed [CW complex](c:cw-complex), and let $J(X)$ be the [free topological monoid](c:free-topological-monoid) on $X$ with the base point as unit. The monoid map $J(X)\to\Omega\Sigma X$ that extends the inclusion of $X$ into the [loop space](c:loop-space) of the [suspension](c:suspension) is a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence).

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a pointed [CW complex](c:cw-complex) whose base point is a vertex.
$X$ is [connected](c:connected-space).

conclusion: $J(X)\to\Omega\Sigma X$ is a weak homotopy equivalence, so $\pi_nJ(X)\cong\pi_{n+1}\Sigma X$ for all $n$.

proofs.name: Homology comparison
proofs.slogan: Compute the homology of both spaces as the tensor algebra on the reduced homology of $X$, compare the monoid map, and conclude with Whitehead's theorem.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the homology of $\Omega\Sigma X$ in step 3 rests on the cited work. Both spaces are connected H-spaces, and the proof first treats field coefficients.

roles.why: The cell structure filters $J(X)$ by word length and gives its homology.
Connectedness makes $\Sigma X$ simply connected and both loop-type spaces connected H-spaces.

steps.slogan: Filter $J(X)$ by word length into pieces whose quotients are smash powers of $X$.
steps.detail: The piece $J_n(X)$ is the image of $X^n$, and $J_n(X)/J_{n-1}(X)\cong X^{\wedge n}$. This is a CW filtration, so $J(X)$ is a CW complex with a monoid structure.

steps.slogan: Compute the homology of $J(X)$ as the [tensor algebra](c:tensor-algebra) on $\tilde H_*(X)$.
steps.detail: The cited work shows that $\Sigma J(X)$ splits as a wedge of the spaces $\Sigma X^{\wedge n}$. With field coefficients the Künneth theorem then gives $\tilde H_*(J(X))\cong\bigoplus_n\tilde H_*(X)^{\otimes n}$, with the product of $J(X)$ acting by concatenation.

steps.slogan: Compute the homology of $\Omega\Sigma X$ from the path fibration over $\Sigma X$.
steps.detail: The cited work runs the Serre spectral sequence of $\Omega\Sigma X\to P\Sigma X\to\Sigma X$, whose total space is contractible. It shows that $H_*(\Omega\Sigma X;k)$ is the tensor algebra $T(\tilde H_*(X;k))$ on the image of $X$ (the Bott-Samelson theorem).

steps.slogan: Show that the monoid map induces an isomorphism on homology.
steps.detail: The map $J(X)\to\Omega\Sigma X$ is a map of [H-spaces](c:h-space) that restricts to the inclusion on $X$. So it induces the algebra map $T(\tilde H_*X)\to T(\tilde H_*X)$ that is the identity on generators, an isomorphism for every field of coefficients and hence over $\mathbb Z$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the map is a weak equivalence by Whitehead's theorem for simple spaces.
steps.detail: Both spaces are connected H-spaces, so they are simple: $\pi_1$ is abelian and acts trivially on the higher homotopy groups. A homology isomorphism of such spaces is a weak homotopy equivalence.

concepts.c:cw-complex: The cell structure gives the filtration of $J(X)$ and its cellular homology.
concepts.c:free-topological-monoid: The James construction is the free monoid on the pointed space $X$.
concepts.c:loop-space: The loop space $\Omega\Sigma X$ is the target of the comparison map.
concepts.c:suspension: The suspension $\Sigma X$ is the base of the path fibration.
concepts.c:weak-homotopy-equivalence: This is the strength of equivalence that the theorem proves.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness of $X$ makes the spaces connected and simple.
concepts.c:tensor-algebra: Both homologies are the tensor algebra on the reduced homology of $X$.
concepts.c:h-space: The monoid structures make both spaces H-spaces, so the map is multiplicative.

source.ref: A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press, 2002, section 4.J (The Loopspace of a Suspension)
source.note: The theorem is due to I. M. James, Reduced product spaces, Annals of Mathematics 62 (1955), 170-197. The outline follows the homology comparison through the Bott-Samelson theorem and Whitehead's theorem.

statement: Let $X$ be a path-connected space. Then there are a [discrete group](c:discrete-group) $G$ and a map $K(G,1)\to X$, from an [Eilenberg-MacLane space](c:eilenberg-maclane-space), that is a [homology equivalence](c:homology-equivalence): it induces isomorphisms on homology with every local coefficient system of $X$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a path-connected topological space.

conclusion: Some discrete group $G$ has a map $K(G,1)\to X$ that is an isomorphism on homology with all local coefficients of $X$.

proofs.name: Gluing acyclic groups over simplices
proofs.slogan: Replace $X$ by a simplicial complex, glue classifying spaces of acyclic groups along its simplices, and show that the glued space is aspherical and homology equivalent to the complex.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published construction; the choice of the acyclic groups and the asphericity in steps 2 and 4 rest on the cited work. The construction is functorial in $X$, which is not shown here.

roles.why: Path-connectedness gives a connected simplicial model and a fundamental group that the glued space inherits.

steps.slogan: Replace $X$ by a connected simplicial complex $K$ with a weak equivalence $|K|\to X$.
steps.detail: Every space is weakly equivalent to a simplicial complex, and a weak equivalence induces isomorphisms on homology with all local coefficients. So it is enough to prove the theorem for $|K|$.

steps.slogan: Attach to each simplex $\sigma$ of $K$ an acyclic group $G_\sigma$, with injective maps along faces.
steps.detail: The cited work builds discrete groups $G_\sigma$, with [acyclic](c:acyclic-group) classifying spaces $BG_\sigma$, and injections $G_\tau\to G_\sigma$ for faces $\tau\subseteq\sigma$. It uses amalgamated products of acyclic groups; every group embeds in an acyclic group.

steps.slogan: Glue the spaces $BG_\sigma$ along the face maps into a [homotopy colimit](c:homotopy-colimit) $T$.
steps.detail: Let $T$ be the homotopy colimit of the diagram $\sigma\mapsto BG_\sigma$ over the poset of simplices. The maps $BG_\sigma\to\{\sigma\}$ to the contractible simplices induce a map $t\colon T\to|K|$.

steps.slogan: Show that $T$ is aspherical, so $T\simeq K(G,1)$ for $G=\pi_1T$.
steps.detail: The cited work arranges the groups and the gluing so that the glued space has contractible universal cover. Then $T$ is a [classifying space](c:classifying-space) of its fundamental group, the [discrete group](c:discrete-group) $G=\pi_1T$.

steps.slogan: Show that $t$ induces isomorphisms on homology with all local coefficients.
steps.detail: The map $t$ is a map of homotopy colimits over one poset, and each piece $BG_\sigma\to\{\sigma\}$ is acyclic. A Mayer-Vietoris or spectral sequence comparison of the two homotopy colimits shows that $t$ is a [homology equivalence](c:homology-equivalence).

steps.slogan: Compose $t$ with the weak equivalence $|K|\to X$ to get the required map.
steps.detail: The composite $K(G,1)\simeq T\to|K|\to X$ is a homology equivalence with every local coefficient system, because both factors are. This is the map of the theorem.

concepts.c:discrete-group: The theorem produces a discrete group $G$ whose classifying space models the homology of $X$.
concepts.c:eilenberg-maclane-space: The space $K(G,1)$ is the aspherical space that replaces $X$ homologically.
concepts.c:homology-equivalence: The map from $K(G,1)$ must be an isomorphism on homology with local coefficients.
concepts.c:acyclic-group: Acyclic groups have the homology of a point, like the simplices they replace.
concepts.c:homotopy-colimit: The glued space is a homotopy colimit, which allows the homology comparison.
concepts.c:classifying-space: An aspherical space is the classifying space of its fundamental group.

source.ref: G. Baumslag, E. Dyer and A. Heller, The topology of discrete groups, Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra 16 (1980), 1-47
source.note: This gives a proof of the theorem of D. M. Kan and W. P. Thurston, Every connected space has the homology of a K(pi,1), Topology 15 (1976), 253-258, with a functorial construction.

statement: Let $H$ be a self-adjoint [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) on a complex Hilbert space, and $\Theta$ an [antiunitary operator](c:antiunitary-operator) with $\Theta H=H\Theta$ and $\Theta^2=-1$, as for [time reversal](c:time-reversal) of a system with half-integer total spin. Then every [eigenspace](c:eigenspace) of $H$ is $\Theta$-invariant, and no eigenspace is one-dimensional.

hypotheses.text: The [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) $H$ is self-adjoint and $\Theta H=H\Theta$.
$\Theta$ is an [antiunitary operator](c:antiunitary-operator): antilinear and bijective, with $\langle\Theta\varphi,\Theta\chi\rangle=\langle\chi,\varphi\rangle$.
$\Theta^2=-1$; this holds for [time reversal](c:time-reversal) when the total spin is half-integer.

conclusion: For each eigenvalue $E$ and eigenvector $\psi$, the vectors $\psi$ and $\Theta\psi$ are orthogonal eigenvectors for $E$, so $E$ has multiplicity at least $2$, and a finite multiplicity is even.

proofs.name: Orthogonal partner
proofs.slogan: Map an eigenvector by $\Theta$ to a second eigenvector of the same energy, and show that the two are orthogonal because $\Theta^2=-1$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The physics input $\Theta^2=(-1)^{2S}$ for total spin $S$ is the hypothesis $\Theta^2=-1$ and is not proved here.

roles.why: Commuting with $H$ makes $\Theta\psi$ an eigenvector with the same eigenvalue.
Antilinearity keeps the eigenvalue real, and the inner product identity drives the orthogonality.
The sign $\Theta^2=-1$ turns the inner product $\langle\Theta\psi,\psi\rangle$ into its own negative.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Theta\psi$ is an eigenvector of $H$ with the same eigenvalue $E$.
steps.detail: Let $H\psi=E\psi$ with $\psi\ne0$. Then $E$ is real because $H$ is self-adjoint, and $\Theta$ is antilinear, so $H\Theta\psi=\Theta H\psi=\Theta(E\psi)=\bar E\,\Theta\psi=E\,\Theta\psi$. Also $\Theta\psi\ne0$ because $\Theta$ preserves norms.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Theta\psi$ is orthogonal to $\psi$.
steps.detail: Take $\varphi=\psi$ and $\chi=\Theta\psi$ in $\langle\Theta\varphi,\Theta\chi\rangle=\langle\chi,\varphi\rangle$ and use $\Theta^2\psi=-\psi$. This gives $-\langle\Theta\psi,\psi\rangle=\langle\Theta\psi,\Theta^2\psi\rangle=\langle\Theta\psi,\psi\rangle$, so $\langle\Theta\psi,\psi\rangle=0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the [eigenspace](c:eigenspace) $V_E$ is $\Theta$-invariant and has dimension at least $2$.
steps.detail: By step 1, $\Theta$ maps $V_E$ into $V_E$. By steps 1 and 2, $\psi$ and $\Theta\psi$ are nonzero orthogonal vectors of $V_E$, hence linearly independent, so $\dim V_E\ge2$.

steps.slogan: Split off the pair $\psi,\Theta\psi$ and repeat in its orthogonal complement.
steps.detail: If $\varphi\perp\psi,\Theta\psi$, then $\langle\Theta\varphi,\psi\rangle=-\langle\Theta\varphi,\Theta(\Theta\psi)\rangle=-\langle\Theta\psi,\varphi\rangle=0$ and $\langle\Theta\varphi,\Theta\psi\rangle=\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle=0$. So the complement of the pair in $V_E$ is $\Theta$-invariant, and induction gives an orthogonal basis of pairs $\psi_j,\Theta\psi_j$ when $\dim V_E$ is finite.

concepts.c:hamiltonian: The Hamiltonian fixes the energy levels whose degeneracy the theorem counts.
concepts.c:antiunitary-operator: Time reversal is antiunitary, which gives antilinearity and the inner product identity.
concepts.c:time-reversal: Time reversal with $\Theta^2=-1$ causes the degeneracy.
concepts.c:eigenspace: The eigenspace of an energy level is the space whose dimension is shown to be even.

source.note: The standard argument of Kramers (1930) and Wigner (1932), as in Sakurai, Modern Quantum Mechanics, chapter 4 on time reversal.

statement: Assume the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice). Then every [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding) $j\colon V\to V$ of the universe of sets into itself is the identity. So there is no [Reinhardt cardinal](c:reinhardt-cardinal) in ZFC.

hypotheses.text: The [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) holds.
$j\colon V\to V$ is an [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding) of the universe of sets into itself.

conclusion: The map $j$ is the identity on $V$.

proofs.name: Critical sequence and a Jónsson function
proofs.slogan: Suppose $j$ moves an ordinal, take the supremum of its critical sequence, and use an $\omega$-Jónsson function on it to find the critical point in the range of $j$.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the combinatorial lemma of step 3 rests on the cited work. The theorem is a scheme over the class $j$, and the same argument shows that $V_{\lambda+2}$ has no nontrivial self-embedding.

roles.why: Elementarity makes $j$ preserve ordinals, sequences and Jónsson functions, so $j(F)$ is again a Jónsson function.
Choice gives the $\omega$-Jónsson function through Kunen's combinatorial lemma.

steps.slogan: Assume $j$ moves an ordinal and build its critical sequence $\kappa_n$.
steps.detail: If $j$ fixes every ordinal, it is the identity by induction on rank. Otherwise let $\kappa$ be the least ordinal with $j(\kappa)>\kappa$, and put $\kappa_0=\kappa$, $\kappa_{n+1}=j(\kappa_n)$. Then $\kappa_n$ increases, and $\kappa$ is not in the range of $j$: if $\kappa=j(\alpha)$ then $\alpha<\kappa$ gives $j(\alpha)=\alpha\ne\kappa$, and $\alpha\ge\kappa$ gives $j(\alpha)>\kappa$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\lambda=\sup_n\kappa_n$ satisfies $j(\lambda)=\lambda$.
steps.detail: Since $j(n)=n$ for each natural number $n$, elementarity gives $j(\langle\kappa_n:n<\omega\rangle)=\langle\kappa_{n+1}:n<\omega\rangle$. So $j(\lambda)=\sup_n\kappa_{n+1}=\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Fix an $\omega$-Jónsson function $F\colon[\lambda]^\omega\to\lambda$ given by Kunen's lemma.
steps.detail: Using the axiom of choice, Kunen's lemma gives $F$ with $F''[A]^\omega=\lambda$ for every $A\subseteq\lambda$ of cardinality $\lambda$. The cited work proves this combinatorial lemma by an Erdős-Hajnal type argument.

steps.slogan: Find a countable $y\subseteq j''\lambda$ with $j(F)(y)=\kappa$.
steps.detail: By elementarity $j(F)$ is an $\omega$-Jónsson function for $j(\lambda)=\lambda$. The set $j''\lambda$ has cardinality $\lambda$ because $j$ is injective, and $\kappa<\lambda$, so some countable $y\subseteq j''\lambda$ has $j(F)(y)=\kappa$.

steps.slogan: Pull $y$ back to a countable $s\subseteq\lambda$ and place $\kappa$ in the range of $j$.
steps.detail: Let $s=j^{-1}[y]$, a countable subset of $\lambda$. For countable $s$ we have $j(s)=j''s=y$. So $\kappa=j(F)(j(s))=j(F(s))$ lies in the range of $j$, which contradicts step 1, and so $j$ fixes every ordinal and is the identity.

concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice is needed for the Jónsson function.
concepts.c:elementary-embedding: Elementarity moves ordinals, sequences and the function $F$ across $j$.
concepts.c:reinhardt-cardinal: A Reinhardt cardinal would be the critical point of such an embedding.

source.ref: A. Kanamori, The Higher Infinite: Large Cardinals in Set Theory from Their Beginnings, 2nd edition, Springer Monographs in Mathematics, Springer, 2003, section 23 (theorem 23.14)
source.note: The theorem is due to K. Kunen, Elementary embeddings and infinitary combinatorics, Journal of Symbolic Logic 36 (1971), 407-413. The outline is the proof with an $\omega$-Jónsson function.

statement: Let $R$ be a ring with a [formal group law](c:formal-group-law), classified by a ring map $MU_*\to R$. Suppose that for every prime $p$ the sequence $p,v_1,v_2,\dots$ is a [regular sequence](c:regular-sequence) on $R$. Then $X\mapsto MU_*(X)\otimes_{MU_*}R$, with $MU_*$ the coefficients of [complex cobordism](c:complex-cobordism), is a homology theory.

hypotheses.text: $R$ carries a [formal group law](c:formal-group-law), that is, an $MU_*$-algebra structure (Lazard's theorem).
For every prime $p$ the images $p,v_1,v_2,\dots$ form a [regular sequence](c:regular-sequence) on $R$, where $v_n$ is the image of the $n$-th generator of $MU_*$ at $p$.

conclusion: The functor $E_*(X)=MU_*(X)\otimes_{MU_*}R$ satisfies the axioms of a homology theory, in particular it sends cofiber sequences to long exact sequences.

proofs.name: Landweber filtration and Tor vanishing
proofs.slogan: Show that tensoring with $R$ is exact on finitely presented comodules by filtering them with the invariant prime ideals, then pass to all complexes by direct limits.
proofs.scope: An outline of Landweber's proof; the filtration theorem of step 3 rests on the cited work. Homotopy invariance and additivity come from $MU_*(-)$, and only exactness needs the regular sequence.

roles.why: The formal group law makes $R$ an $MU_*$-module and fixes the images $v_n\in R$.
The regular sequence kills higher Tor against the quotients $MU_*/I_{p,n}$.

steps.slogan: Turn the formal group law into an $MU_*$-module structure on $R$.
steps.detail: By Lazard's theorem and Quillen's identification of $MU_*$ with the Lazard ring, the formal group law is classified by a ring map $MU_*\to R$. This makes $R$ an $MU_*$-module and fixes the images $v_n\in R$.

steps.slogan: Reduce exactness of $E_*$ on finite complexes to exactness of $R\otimes-$ on comodules.
steps.detail: For a finite complex $X$, $MU_*(X)$ is a finitely presented comodule over $MU_*MU$. Homotopy invariance and additivity pass from $MU_*(-)$ to $E_*$, so it remains to show that $R\otimes_{MU_*}-$ is exact on exact sequences of such [comodules](c:comodule).

steps.slogan: Filter a finitely presented comodule by the invariant prime ideals.
steps.detail: Landweber's filtration theorem gives every finitely presented $MU_*MU$-comodule $N$ a finite filtration by subcomodules whose quotients are suspensions $\Sigma^dMU_*/I_{p,n}$ with $I_{p,n}=(p,v_1,\dots,v_{n-1})$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathrm{Tor}_i^{MU_*}(MU_*/I_{p,n},R)=0$ for $i>0$.
steps.detail: The sequence $p,v_1,\dots,v_{n-1}$ is regular on $MU_*$, so its Koszul complex resolves $MU_*/I_{p,n}$. It is regular on $R$, so the Koszul complex of $R$ has no homology in positive degrees. These homology groups are the Tor groups.

steps.slogan: Climb the filtration to get exactness of $R\otimes-$ on finitely presented comodules.
steps.detail: Long exact sequences of Tor and induction on the filtration length give $\mathrm{Tor}_1^{MU_*}(N,R)=0$ for every finitely presented comodule $N$. So $R\otimes_{MU_*}-$ is exact on these comodules, and $E_*$ takes cofiber sequences of finite complexes to long exact sequences.

steps.slogan: Pass from finite complexes to all complexes by direct limits.
steps.detail: A CW complex is the directed union of its finite subcomplexes. The functors $MU_*(-)$ and $R\otimes_{MU_*}-$ commute with directed colimits, and directed colimits of exact sequences are exact. So $E_*$ is exact and additive on all CW complexes, a homology theory.

concepts.c:formal-group-law: The formal group law is the input that makes $R$ an $MU_*$-module.
concepts.c:regular-sequence: Regularity of $p,v_1,\dots$ on $R$ is what makes the Tor groups vanish.
concepts.c:complex-cobordism: Complex cobordism supplies the homology theory that is tensored with $R$.
concepts.c:comodule: The homology $MU_*(X)$ of a finite complex is a comodule, which the filtration theorem studies.

source.ref: P. S. Landweber, Homological properties of comodules over MU_*(MU) and BP_*(BP), American Journal of Mathematics 98 (1976), no. 3, 591-610
source.note: The paper proves the filtration theorem for finitely presented comodules and deduces the exact functor theorem from it.

statement: Let $f$ be even and $g$ odd, both continuously differentiable, with $g(x)>0$ for $x>0$, and let $F(x)=\int_0^xf$. Suppose $F$ has exactly one positive zero $a$, with $F<0$ on $(0,a)$, and $F$ is positive, increasing and unbounded on $(a,\infty)$. Then $\ddot x+f(x)\dot x+g(x)=0$ has exactly one [limit cycle](c:limit-cycle), and it is stable.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is even and $g$ is odd, and both are continuously differentiable.
$g(x)>0$ for every $x>0$.
$F(x)=\int_0^xf$ has exactly one positive zero $a$, satisfies $F<0$ on $(0,a)$, and is positive, increasing and unbounded on $(a,\infty)$.

conclusion: The equation has exactly one closed orbit in the phase plane; this [limit cycle](c:limit-cycle) encloses the origin and is orbitally stable.

proofs.name: Liénard plane and half-return map
proofs.slogan: Pass to the Liénard plane, follow orbits through a half turn, and show that the energy change of the half turn has exactly one zero, where it changes sign.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the return-map and monotonicity estimates of steps 3 and 4 rest on the cited work. Half turns suffice, because the symmetry of step 1 gives the other half.

roles.why: Parity makes $F$ odd and gives the symmetry $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$, so a half turn determines the whole orbit.
The sign of $g$ gives a unique equilibrium and a positive energy $G$.
The sign pattern of $F$ makes the energy grow near the origin and shrink far away.

steps.slogan: Pass to the Liénard plane $\dot x=y-F(x)$, $\dot y=-g(x)$.
steps.detail: Setting $y=\dot x+F(x)$ turns the second order equation into this system. Its only equilibrium is the origin, because $g$ vanishes only at $0$ and $F(0)=0$. It is invariant under $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$ because $F$ and $g$ are odd.

steps.slogan: Show that $v=y^2/2+G(x)$ grows along orbits in the strip $|x|<a$.
steps.detail: With $G(x)=\int_0^xg$ we get $\dot v=-g(x)F(x)$, which is positive for $0<|x|<a$ by the signs of $g$ and $F$. So the origin repels, and no closed orbit lies inside the strip.

steps.slogan: Follow an orbit from $(0,\alpha)$ through a half turn to $(0,-\beta(\alpha))$.
steps.detail: The cited work shows that orbits circle the origin clockwise and cross the $y$-axis alternately above and below. By the symmetry of step 1, closed orbits correspond to fixed points $\beta(\alpha)=\alpha$ of the half-return map.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Delta(\alpha)=\int F(x)\,dy$ over the half orbit has one sign change.
steps.detail: We have $\Delta=v(0,-\beta)-v(0,\alpha)$, and $\Delta=0$ exactly when $\beta=\alpha$. By step 2, $\Delta>0$ for small $\alpha$. The cited work shows that $\Delta$ is strictly decreasing once the orbit passes $x=a$, and $\Delta\to-\infty$ as $\alpha\to\infty$, so $\Delta$ has exactly one zero $\alpha_0$.

steps.slogan: Read the unique zero $\alpha_0$ as the unique closed orbit.
steps.detail: The orbit through $(0,\alpha_0)$ returns to $(0,-\alpha_0)$, and by the symmetry it closes up. Every closed orbit surrounds the origin and meets the $y$-axis at such a point, so there is exactly one closed orbit.

steps.slogan: Show that the closed orbit attracts nearby orbits.
steps.detail: For $\alpha<\alpha_0$ we have $\Delta>0$, so $\beta(\alpha)>\alpha$, and the return points increase but stay below $\alpha_0$, because orbits cannot cross the closed orbit. Their limit is a fixed point of the continuous half-return map, so it is $\alpha_0$. For $\alpha>\alpha_0$ the points decrease to $\alpha_0$ in the same way, so the limit cycle is stable.

concepts.c:limit-cycle: The theorem counts isolated closed orbits and shows that the one orbit attracts nearby orbits.

source.ref: L. Perko, Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, 3rd edition, Texts in Applied Mathematics 7, Springer, 2001, section 3.8 (Liénard systems)
source.note: The theorem is due to A. Liénard, Étude des oscillations entretenues, Revue générale de l'électricité 23 (1928), 901-912 and 946-954.

statement: For every complex number $z$ with $|z|<1$, the [power series](c:power-series) $\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}z^n/n$ converges absolutely, and its sum is $\log(1+z)$, where $\log$ is the principal [logarithm](c:logarithm).

hypotheses.text: The complex number $z$ satisfies $|z|<1$.

formal.difference: mathlib states the sum over all $n\ge0$ with the term at $n=0$ equal to $0$, because division by zero is $0$; the sum is the same.

proofs.name: Taylor remainder along a segment
proofs.slogan: Bound the difference between the logarithm and its Taylor polynomial by integrating its derivative along the segment from $0$ to $z$, then let the degree grow.
proofs.scope: The principal branch on the disc $|z|<1$, where $1+z$ lies in the right half plane. The case $z=0$ is trivial.

roles.why: The disc keeps $1+tz$ away from $0$ with $|1+tz|\ge1-|z|$, and makes the geometric series converge.

steps.slogan: Show that the series converges absolutely by comparison with a geometric series.
steps.detail: For $n\ge1$ we have $|z^n/n|\le|z|^n$, and $\sum|z|^n$ is a [geometric series](c:geometric-series) with ratio less than $1$. So the series [converges absolutely](c:absolute-convergence), and its sum does not depend on the order of the terms.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the difference $d_n(w)=\log(1+w)-T_{n+1}(w)$ of the logarithm and its Taylor polynomial.
steps.detail: Here $T_{n+1}(w)=\sum_{j=1}^n(-1)^{j+1}w^j/j$, whose derivative is $\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-w)^j$. The finite geometric sum then gives $d_n'(w)=\frac1{1+w}-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-w)^j=\frac{(-w)^n}{1+w}$, and $d_n(0)=0$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the derivative along the segment from $0$ to $z$.
steps.detail: Since $d_n(0)=0$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $d_n(z)=z\int_0^1\frac{(-tz)^n}{1+tz}\,dt$. The segment stays in the disc, where $|1+tz|\ge1-|z|$.

steps.slogan: Bound the remainder by $|z|^{n+1}/((n+1)(1-|z|))$.
steps.detail: The modulus of the integrand is at most $t^n/(1-|z|)$ because $|1+tz|\ge1-|z|$. So $|d_n(z)|\le|z|^{n+1}\int_0^1\frac{t^n}{1-|z|}\,dt=\frac{|z|^{n+1}}{(n+1)(1-|z|)}$.

steps.slogan: Let $n$ grow to identify the sum of the series with $\log(1+z)$.
steps.detail: The value $T_{n+1}(z)$ is the $n$-th partial sum of the series. The bound of step 4 tends to $0$ because $|z|<1$, so the partial sums converge to $\log(1+z)$, and by step 1 this is the sum of the series.

concepts.c:power-series: The statement is the power series expansion of $\log(1+z)$ at $0$.
concepts.c:logarithm: The principal logarithm is the function that the series represents.
concepts.c:geometric-series: The finite geometric sum gives the derivative, and the infinite one gives convergence.
concepts.c:absolute-convergence: Absolute convergence makes the sum independent of the order of terms.

source.note: mathlib bounds the remainder in Complex.norm_log_sub_logTaylor_le, by integrating hasDerivAt_log_sub_logTaylor along the segment, and compares the series with the geometric series of $\|z\|^n$.

statement: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be [independent](c:independence) random variables with means $\mu_i$, variances $\sigma_i^2>0$ and finite [moments](c:moment) $E|X_i-\mu_i|^{2+\delta}$ for some $\delta>0$. Put $s_n^2=\sum_{i\le n}\sigma_i^2$. If $s_n^{-(2+\delta)}\sum_{i\le n}E|X_i-\mu_i|^{2+\delta}\to0$, then $s_n^{-1}\sum_{i\le n}(X_i-\mu_i)$ [converges in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to the standard [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution).

hypotheses.text: The random variables $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are [independent](c:independence).
For some $\delta>0$ each $X_i$ has finite [moment](c:moment) $E|X_i-\mu_i|^{2+\delta}$ and variance $\sigma_i^2>0$.
Lyapunov's condition holds: $s_n^{-(2+\delta)}\sum_{i\le n}E|X_i-\mu_i|^{2+\delta}\to0$.

conclusion: The normalized sums $s_n^{-1}\sum_{i\le n}(X_i-\mu_i)$ converge in distribution to $N(0,1)$.

proofs.name: Characteristic functions
proofs.slogan: Compare the characteristic function of the normalized sum with a product of Gaussian factors, and use Lyapunov's condition to control every error term.
proofs.scope: The proof treats $0<\delta\le1$ in the Taylor step and reduces larger $\delta$ to $\delta=1$ by Hölder's inequality. Lindeberg's theorem is the more general result and is not used.

roles.why: Independence turns the characteristic function of the sum into a product of characteristic functions.
Finite moments and positive variances make $s_n>0$ and the Taylor remainders finite.
Lyapunov's condition makes the sum of the remainders tend to zero and makes every variance small.

steps.slogan: Normalize the summands and show that every variance becomes small.
steps.detail: Put $Y_{ni}=(X_i-\mu_i)/s_n$, so $EY_{ni}=0$ and $\sum_iEY_{ni}^2=1$. If $\delta>1$, Hölder's inequality gives $\sum_iE|Y_{ni}|^3\le(\sum_iE|Y_{ni}|^{2+\delta})^{1/\delta}\to0$, so we take $\delta\le1$. Then $\sigma_{ni}^2=EY_{ni}^2\le(E|Y_{ni}|^{2+\delta})^{2/(2+\delta)}$ gives $\max_i\sigma_{ni}^2\to0$.

steps.slogan: Expand each [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) to second order with a $|t|^{2+\delta}$ remainder.
steps.detail: For real $x$ and $0<\delta\le1$ we have $|e^{ix}-1-ix+x^2/2|\le\min(|x|^3/6,x^2)\le|x|^{2+\delta}$. With $EY_{ni}=0$ this gives $|\varphi_{ni}(t)-(1-t^2\sigma_{ni}^2/2)|\le|t|^{2+\delta}E|Y_{ni}|^{2+\delta}$, where $\varphi_{ni}$ is the characteristic function of $Y_{ni}$.

steps.slogan: Compare the product of the characteristic functions with the product of the quadratic factors.
steps.detail: For complex numbers of modulus at most $1$, $|\prod a_i-\prod b_i|\le\sum|a_i-b_i|$. Independence gives $Ee^{it\sum_iY_{ni}}=\prod_i\varphi_{ni}(t)$. For fixed $t$ and large $n$ the factors $1-t^2\sigma_{ni}^2/2$ lie in $[0,1]$, so the product differs from $\prod_i\varphi_{ni}(t)$ by at most $|t|^{2+\delta}\sum_iE|Y_{ni}|^{2+\delta}\to0$.

steps.slogan: Replace each quadratic factor $1-x_i$ by $e^{-x_i}$ and use $\sum_i\sigma_{ni}^2=1$.
steps.detail: With $x_i=t^2\sigma_{ni}^2/2\in[0,1]$ we have $|e^{-x_i}-(1-x_i)|\le x_i^2$, so $|\prod e^{-x_i}-\prod(1-x_i)|\le\sum x_i^2\le\frac{t^4}4\max_i\sigma_{ni}^2\to0$. Since $\prod e^{-x_i}=e^{-t^2/2}$, we get $\prod_i\varphi_{ni}(t)\to e^{-t^2/2}$.

steps.slogan: Apply Lévy's continuity theorem to get convergence in distribution.
steps.detail: The characteristic functions of $s_n^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\mu_i)$ converge pointwise to $e^{-t^2/2}$, the characteristic function of $N(0,1)$, which is continuous at $0$. Lévy's continuity theorem gives the convergence in distribution.

concepts.c:independence: Independence factorizes the characteristic function of the sum.
concepts.c:convergence-in-distribution: This is the mode of convergence that the theorem proves.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: The limit law is the standard normal law, with characteristic function $e^{-t^2/2}$.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: The proof compares characteristic functions instead of distributions.

source.note: The characteristic function proof of Lyapunov's theorem, as in Billingsley, Probability and Measure, section 27.

statement: Let $X$ be a finite set and $\mathcal A$ a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) of subsets of $X$. Then $|\mathcal A|\le|\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal A|$, where $\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal A=\{a\setminus b:a,b\in\mathcal A\}$.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal A$ is a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) of subsets of a finite set $X$.

conclusion: The family of differences $a\setminus b$ with $a,b\in\mathcal A$ has at least $|\mathcal A|$ members.

formal.difference: mathlib proves it for a finite family in any generalized Boolean algebra, of which families of subsets of a finite set are the standard case.

proofs.name: Four functions theorem
proofs.slogan: Derive $|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|\le|\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal B||\mathcal B\setminus\mathcal A|$ from the four functions theorem with the complement family, then set $\mathcal B=\mathcal A$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement; for the empty family both sides are $0$.

roles.why: A finite ground set makes the four functions theorem apply, and finiteness makes the counts finite.

steps.slogan: Specialize the four functions theorem to constant functions to get Daykin's inequality.
steps.detail: The Ahlswede-Daykin inequality says that $f_1(a)f_2(b)\le f_3(a\cap b)f_4(a\cup b)$ for all $a,b$ implies $f_1(\mathcal A)f_2(\mathcal B)\le f_3(\mathcal A\wedge\mathcal B)f_4(\mathcal A\vee\mathcal B)$, where $f(\mathcal C)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C}f(c)$. With all four functions equal to $1$ it gives $|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|\le|\mathcal A\wedge\mathcal B||\mathcal A\vee\mathcal B|$, where $\mathcal A\wedge\mathcal B=\{a\cap b\}$ and $\mathcal A\vee\mathcal B=\{a\cup b\}$.

steps.slogan: Replace $\mathcal B$ by the family $\mathcal B^c$ of complements.
steps.detail: Put $\mathcal B^c=\{X\setminus b:b\in\mathcal B\}$, so that $|\mathcal B^c|=|\mathcal B|$. Daykin's inequality for $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B^c$ reads $|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|\le|\mathcal A\wedge\mathcal B^c||\mathcal A\vee\mathcal B^c|$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite both factors on the right as families of differences.
steps.detail: We have $a\cap(X\setminus b)=a\setminus b$, so $|\mathcal A\wedge\mathcal B^c|=|\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal B|$. Also $a\cup(X\setminus b)=X\setminus(b\setminus a)$, so $\mathcal A\vee\mathcal B^c$ is the family of complements of $\mathcal B\setminus\mathcal A$ and has $|\mathcal B\setminus\mathcal A|$ members. Hence $|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|\le|\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal B||\mathcal B\setminus\mathcal A|$.

steps.slogan: Take $\mathcal B=\mathcal A$ and extract the square root.
steps.detail: Then both difference families equal $\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal A$, so $|\mathcal A|^2\le|\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal A|^2$. Both sizes are nonnegative, so $|\mathcal A|\le|\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal A|$.

concepts.c:family-of-sets: The inequality compares a family of sets with its family of differences.

source.note: mathlib proves le_card_diffs_mul_card_diffs from the Daykin inequality le_card_infs_mul_card_sups (the four functions theorem with constant functions) applied to the complement family, then takes a square root with le_of_pow_le_pow_left₀.

statement: Let $K\subset\mathbb C$ be [compact](c:compact-space) with [connected](c:connected-space) complement, and let $f$ be continuous on $K$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) in the interior of $K$. Then for every $\varepsilon>0$ some polynomial $P$ satisfies $|f-P|<\varepsilon$ on $K$.

hypotheses.text: $K\subset\mathbb C$ is [compact](c:compact-space).
The complement $\mathbb C\setminus K$ is [connected](c:connected-space).
$f$ is continuous on $K$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) in the interior of $K$.

conclusion: The function $f$ is a [uniform](c:uniform-convergence) limit on $K$ of polynomials.

proofs.name: Cauchy transform and kernel replacement
proofs.slogan: Reduce to rational approximation, smooth the extension of $f$ at a small scale, write it as a Cauchy integral, and replace the kernel near the boundary by approximable kernels.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the kernel replacement of step 4 and the estimate of step 5 rest on the cited work. The case of empty interior is included; then $f$ is only assumed continuous.

roles.why: Compactness gives a modulus of continuity and a compact support for the extension of $f$.
A connected complement lets Runge's theorem push poles to infinity and makes the kernel replacement possible.
Holomorphy in the interior makes the $\bar\partial$ of the smoothing vanish away from the boundary.

steps.slogan: Reduce the theorem to approximation by rational functions with poles outside $K$.
steps.detail: Because $\mathbb C\setminus K$ is connected, Runge's theorem moves each pole of such a rational function to infinity, uniformly on $K$, and gives polynomials. So it is enough to approximate $f$ uniformly on $K$ by rational functions with poles in $\mathbb C\setminus K$.

steps.slogan: Extend $f$ to a compactly supported function and smooth it at scale $\delta$.
steps.detail: Extend $f$ continuously to $\mathbb C$ with compact support, with modulus of continuity $\omega$. The cited work builds a $C^1$ function $F_\delta$ with $|f-F_\delta|\le\omega(\delta)$ and $|\bar\partial F_\delta|\le C\omega(\delta)/\delta$, and $\bar\partial F_\delta=0$ at points of $K$ farther than $\delta$ from $\partial K$.

steps.slogan: Write $F_\delta$ as a Cauchy integral of $\bar\partial F_\delta$.
steps.detail: For a compactly supported $C^1$ function, $F_\delta(z)=-\frac1\pi\iint\frac{\bar\partial F_\delta(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\,dA(\zeta)$. So $F_\delta$ is an integral of the kernels $1/(\zeta-z)$ over the set where $\bar\partial F_\delta\ne0$, against a density of size at most $C\omega(\delta)/\delta$.

steps.slogan: Replace the kernel $1/(\zeta-z)$ for $\zeta$ near $\partial K$ by kernels in the closure of the rational functions.
steps.detail: This is the heart of the cited proof. Where the pole $\zeta$ lies far from $K$ the kernel already is rational with a pole off $K$. Near $\partial K$ the cited work uses the connectedness of the complement, with conformal mappings, to build replacements that are uniform limits of rational functions with poles off $K$.

steps.slogan: Estimate the error by $C\omega(\delta)$ and let $\delta$ tend to zero.
steps.detail: The replaced kernels differ from the Cauchy kernel by an integrable amount of order $\delta$ on the support of $\bar\partial F_\delta$. With the density bound $C\omega(\delta)/\delta$, the total error is at most $C\omega(\delta)$. So $f$ is within $(1+C)\omega(\delta)\to0$ of the closure of the rational functions with poles off $K$.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness gives the modulus of continuity and the compact support.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness of the complement is the topological hypothesis of the kernel replacement.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy in the interior removes the $\bar\partial$ term away from the boundary.

source.ref: W. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd edition, McGraw-Hill, 1987, chapter 20, theorem 20.5
source.note: The theorem is due to S. N. Mergelyan, Uniform approximations to functions of a complex variable, Uspekhi Matematicheskikh Nauk 7 (1952), no. 2, 31-122.
